about.name: Felipe Caceres - Fernandez
about.bio: Hey my name is Felipe and I'm working towards making a difference in the world through humanoid robotics. I'm an undergrad in Computational Physics at Carnegie Mellon University. Physics teaches you to reason about how the world works from first principles and computer science trains you to analyze problems with math, logic, and abstraction. I'm drawn to humanoid robotics because it pushes the limits of what we can build and forces you to problem solve in many different technical fields.

about_me: I'm from California, and after being admitted to CMU, I took a gap year to live outside an institution while I still had few responsibilities. I chose to focus exclusively on art, learning videography and working on everything from Jubilee episodes to an NYU thesis film shot overnight across New York. I'm also really into calisthenics, soccer, Star Trek, and 80s and house music.

experience.org: Origami Robotics (Humanoid Robotics Startup, YC W26)
experience.one_liner: Owned full-stack development of tactile sensing for dextrous manipulation
experience.description: Owned full-stack development of tactile sensing for dextrous manipulation

feature_photo.alt: Soldering at the workbench while developing the tactile sensors

sections.label: why?
paragraphs: I chose to work for Origami Robotics because they were incredibly aligned with my technical interests and are an up-and-coming startup with a smart team. I was also incredibly interested in the specific role and project I worked on — developing sensors for dextrous robotic hands.

sections.label: what is it?
paragraphs: At Origami, I developed a tactile sensing system applicable to our robotic hand and data-collection device. I organized my internship work in three phases.
Phase 1 — I recreated and familiarized myself with the open-source research project FlexiTac from Columbia University by Binghao Huang.
Phase 2 — I conducted a study on 9 different piezoresistive sensors I designed to understand how altering transducer parameters affected the balance of resolution and reliability.

Phase 3 (where most of my time was spent) — I designed a complete sensing system for our robotic hand and data-collection device. In total I explored three fundamentally different solutions, since designing the high-level architecture of tactile sensing for a hand means deciding where you lie on the spectrum from “centralized” to “localized.” By centralized I mean an architecture that controls and processes sensing for dedicated sensing zones all on one central board — every trace eventually has to get routed from its sensing zone back to that central PCB. By localized I mean an architecture where the control and processing happens at essentially the same location as the sensing zone itself, so each zone is handled by an independent device and data gets acquired from all of them to form a full tactile image.
About piezoresistive-based tactile arrays in general:

sections.label: interesting thoughts
paragraphs: Working on this project made me realize how incredible our bodies are, especially our hands and skin. The amount of capability “packed” into our hands is astounding — they're a marvel of engineering, and our technology isn't advanced enough to fully replicate it. As a result, while working on these problems we constantly have to ask ourselves: “what's the solution that gets me 80% of the capability I need?” For example, I could try to build a sensing system that gives us data about every square millimeter of the hand, but we'd get 80% of the capability of “robotic skin” by just sensing 15 areas on the palm and fingers (and if you think about it, we basically only use our fingertips for most manipulation tasks anyway). This question of choosing the scale at which we mimic our biology is always grounded in the root purpose of the thing we're building — so we need a very clear understanding of that purpose, or we'll end up making decisions that optimize for the wrong thing.

projects.title: Torque-Controlled Robot Joint
projects.one_liner: A robot joint built from fundamental components that measures and controls its own output torque.
projects.description: A robot joint built from fundamental components that measures and controls its own output torque.

sections.label: why?
paragraphs: Sensing and actuation are how a robot's machine learning model touches reality: sensors are how it perceives the world, and actuators are how its decisions become physical action. At Origami I built the sensing side. Here I'm building both, to understand them deeply enough to innovate on them.

sections.label: what is it?
paragraphs: Estimating a joint's torque from motor current is imperfect, because energy is lost in hard-to-predict ways such as gearbox friction. This joint measures its real output torque with a strain-gauge sensor, compares it against the current-based estimate, uses the measurement to control the joint, and yields when pushed by hand.

sections.label: how it works
paragraphs: Sensor: strain-gauge load cell, then an instrumentation amplifier, an offset stage, and an anti-alias filter into the microcontroller's ADC. Motor driver: a three-phase inverter from six MOSFETs with gate drivers, current sensing, a magnetic encoder, and field-oriented control on an STM32. Joint: a 3D-printed cycloidal gearbox from Berkeley's open-source Humanoid Lite.

sections.label: status
paragraphs: Design complete and all components chosen; the build is underway. Full write-up coming as it progresses.

projects.title: 4-DOF Stepper Arm
projects.one_liner: 4-DOF robotic arm built from salvaged 3D printer steppers
projects.description: 4-DOF robotic arm built from salvaged 3D printer steppers

sections.label: overview
paragraphs: A custom 4-DOF arm driven by the stepper motors from my old Creality CR-10, with printed harmonic drive gearboxes and closed-loop drivers. Built with a mechanical engineering friend, the goal is a cheap, maintainable arm designed from scratch around four NEMA 17 steppers salvaged from a Creality CR-10. Links, joint layout, and end effector are custom and expected to go through several iterations.

sections.label: hardware
paragraphs: Each joint uses a printable Robrotics HDP30 harmonic drive (30:1). Motors run on MKS SERVO42D closed-loop drivers, commanded over STEP/DIR from an ESP32, powered by a 12 V 5 A supply. No belts anywhere.

sections.label: status
paragraphs: Currently on single-joint bring-up: one gearbox on one motor, verifying driver calibration and motion before scaling to all four joints.

projects.title: Adjustable Bench Power Supply
projects.one_liner: Custom bench power supply built from a switching supply and buck converter for adjustable, current-limited output
projects.description: Custom bench power supply built from a switching supply and buck converter for adjustable, current-limited output

photos.alt: Adjustable Bench Power Supply on a shelf
Adjustable Bench Power Supply enclosure open, showing the internal wiring

sections.label: why?
paragraphs: The purpose of this project was to learn more about power electronics and to create an adjustable bench power supply for future electronics projects. I had also salvaged a power supply from my old Creality CR-10 3D printer, so I wanted to put it to use in a project.

sections.label: what is it?
paragraphs: I built an adjustable bench supply from the 12 V / 30 A switching supply (SMPS) salvaged from my Creality CR-10. It feeds a DPS5005 CC/CV buck module (CC/CV: it regulates either constant current or constant voltage, whichever limit is hit first). The output is 0 to about 10.5 V and 0 to 5 A, with live voltage and current shown on the module's LCD.

sections.label: problem solving
paragraphs: The biggest problem I ran into with this project was actually the enclosure, not the electronics — the wiring was simple and everything worked on the first try (which never happens). I first designed an enclosure to be laser cut from acrylic using an online DXF generator, modified in Onshape. For some reason the units the online tool generated were incorrect, so the box came out oversized. I still laser cut the parts anyway, because I wanted a complete first version to test the whole thing together, rather than trying to perfect every part before combining them — building a smaller-scale, complete version teaches you more than spending all your energy getting one part exactly right on the first try, which is nearly impossible without an unreasonable amount of knowledge and experience. Once I confirmed everything worked, I designed a second enclosure to be 3D printed, which is more compact and looks better.
I also went with the DPS5005 buck module instead of the DPS5015 to cut cost, since 5 A is plenty for most bench supply uses.

sections.label: why?
paragraphs: "Booth" is a very big tradition at CMU that involves building multi-story houses around a theme. The work for Booth spans about a semester and is generally split into two categories: crafts and structure. Crafts refers to all the art that expresses the ideas in the theme, including robotic decorations, visual elements, and interactive activities. Structure refers to the structural design of the house, which needs to get safety-certified since people at Spring Carnival walk through every booth.

This year I was a room chair, meaning I led all the crafts for one of the rooms. The sub-theme of my room was cassettes, so the aesthetic I was going for was like an 80's teen boy's room. A lot of the inspiration for the room came from Ready Player One and Guardians of the Galaxy.
